reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: An organic acidaemia caused by deficient methylmalonyl-CoA mutase activity or by defects in its adenosylcobalamin (vitamin B12) cofactor synthesis
Typical neonatal presentation is metabolic decompensation with poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, hypotonia and a severe high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis
Characteristic laboratory findings include ketosis, hyperammonaemia, hypoglycaemia, and cytopenias such as neutropenia and thrombocytopenia
Elevated methylmalonic acid in blood and urine with raised propionylcarnitine (C3) on acylcarnitine profile establishes the diagnosis
Long-term complications include chronic kidney disease (tubulointerstitial nephropathy), a movement disorder from basal ganglia injury, growth failure and pancreatitis
Some cobalamin-responsive forms improve with vitamin B12 (hydroxocobalamin), so a cofactor trial is standard

Chronic management principles are a protein-restricted diet limiting propiogenic amino acids, carnitine supplementation and avoidance of catabolism, with metronidazole sometimes used to reduce gut propionate production
Detectable through newborn screening by elevated C3 acylcarnitine, prompting confirmatory testing
reference.pathophysiology: Methylmalonic acidemia results from a block in the conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA, a step catalysed by methylmalonyl-CoA mutase using adenosylcobalamin. This reaction lies on the final common pathway for catabolism of the branched-chain amino acids isoleucine and valine, methionine, threonine, odd-chain fatty acids and cholesterol side chains. Enzyme deficiency or impaired cofactor synthesis causes methylmalonic acid and related organic acids to accumulate, producing severe metabolic acidosis. These metabolites inhibit ureagenesis (causing secondary hyperammonaemia) and mitochondrial energy metabolism, are toxic to bone marrow and renal tubules, and injure the basal ganglia during decompensation.
additionalDifferentials: Propionic acidemia and other organic acidaemias
Urea cycle disorders (hyperammonaemia without high anion gap acidosis)
Acquired vitamin B12 deficiency (in later-onset or maternal cases)
additionalInvestigations: Blood gas and anion gap, blood glucose, lactate and ammonia
Plasma and urine organic acids showing elevated methylmalonic acid
Vitamin B12 responsiveness testing and complementation/molecular studies to subtype
Renal function monitoring and neuroimaging after metabolic crises
redFlags: Acute metabolic decompensation with severe high-anion-gap acidosis is a life-threatening emergency
Hyperammonaemia with encephalopathy accompanying an acidotic crisis
Rapid deterioration during intercurrent illness, fasting or increased protein catabolism
Progressive renal impairment or acute basal ganglia injury with a new movement disorder
reference.prognosis: Prognosis varies by subtype; cobalamin-responsive forms generally do better, whereas mutase-deficient disease carries significant risk of recurrent metabolic crises, chronic kidney disease and neurological injury, and severe cases may require kidney or combined liver-kidney transplantation. Early screening detection and meticulous metabolic control improve outcomes.
pitfalls: Attributing an acidotic, unwell neonate to sepsis and delaying metabolic investigation
Failing to trial and document vitamin B12 responsiveness
Overlooking evolving chronic kidney disease during long-term follow-up
Under-treating catabolism during intercurrent illness, allowing preventable decompensation
management: Institute a protein-restricted diet limiting the propiogenic precursors isoleucine, valine, methionine, and threonine, supplemented with a specialised metabolic formula
Trial parenteral hydroxocobalamin and continue it long-term in cobalamin-responsive forms
Supplement with L-carnitine and consider intermittent gut-flora suppression with metronidazole to reduce propionate production

Manage acute decompensation by stopping protein, giving intravenous glucose with insulin to reverse catabolism, correcting acidosis, and using ammonia scavengers with haemofiltration or dialysis for severe hyperammonaemia
Provide an emergency sick-day regimen and strict fasting avoidance
Undertake surveillance for chronic kidney disease, basal ganglia injury and movement disorder, growth failure, and pancreatitis
Consider liver or combined liver-kidney transplantation in severe or recurrently decompensating disease, with genetic counselling and metabolic multidisciplinary care
